articleTitle: An electric field aid to underwater navigation
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The electric field apparatus described is an economical and convenient aid to restricted area undersea navigation. The asymmetry of an electric dipole is a weighted and comparative indication of the effective clearance of large obstacles.

articleTitle: Numerical simulation of water quality in coastal waters and estuaries
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Assessment of the influence of waste discharges in estuaries necessary for water quality management in these waters. The model described here was developed for well-mixed estuaries and coastal seas in which salinity distributions at any point are uniform over the vertical. Well-mixed regions generally occur when considerable tidal flow exists together with a limited flow of fresh water.

articleTitle: Augmentation of wave measurements by use of a submerged solar cell
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: In a 1957 paper, Schenck (1) noted that a trochoidal water wave having perpendicular sunlight incident upon it would focus this sunlight underwater, maximum focus occuring at depths depending on the wave parameters. A maximum of up to eight times the incident intensity was predicted for the case of zero absorption loss in the water column. Meunz and Marchello ( 2 ) used this approach in the measurement of the height of small, - I capillary waves. Other studies (3,4) have considered the effect of wave-focused light from a statistical or time-average standpoint.

articleTitle: Sea water flooded electric motor for 13,200 PSI
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper describes the design, detaanidl s construction of a 7.5 HP, 30 Hertz, 8 pole, 600 RRM free flooded induction motor. Sea water is used for lubrication of bearings and as a cooling medium.

articleTitle: FMEA - Reliability tool and management aid on Scuba
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: One of the most useful tools for evaluating the reliability and safety aspects of a life support system is the Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA). Using this technique an analyst develops an orderly assessment of the cause, effect, and possible prevention of potential equipment failures. The analysis produces a unified document listing potential failures and causes which are studied at the system level. When used early in the design stages, recommendations for corrective actions can be economically incorporated. This work describes how Westinghouse Ocean Research and Engineering center engineers use the following procedure to analyze failure modes and their effects on a system during the early design stages. The analysis begins with the preparation of a block diagram showing the interrelation of all components in each sub-system and the input and output of the subsystem. A subsystem breakdown for a typical SCUBA shows three diagrams: (1) gas system, (2) electrical system, (3) water system. Each component becomes a subject for analysis. Next, worksheets are prepared for each listed component. The worksheets form the analysis documentation and contain the following information: mode, effect, cause, and prevention. After evaluation of the complete system, the finalized document is presented to management as a tangible acknowledgement of their requirements to produce safe, reliable equipment. The Failure Modes and Effects Analysis thus evolves into a management tool. A tool that serves to provide the impetus for insuring that all conceivable failures are considered and resolved as well as a tool for insuring the embodiment of failure prevention methods into system documentation.

articleTitle: A coding scheme for underwater digital data transmission
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: In this report, considerations on the probability of applying Fibonacci code to underwater data transmission, on its synchronization problems [digit word and frame synchronizations] and on its error detecting or correcting ability are presented and discussed.

articleTitle: Further evaluation of diver communication systems
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This investigation was conducted as part of a program of research involving six experiments; they are designed 1) to develop methodologies for the evaluation of diver communication systems and 2) to carry out evaluations on available units. The data from a previous study, using a diver-to-surface technique, are reviewed briefly as is the methodology of the third project (being carried out at TEKTITE-2 but not yet completed) which includes range and salt water as variables. The major focus of this second experiment is on a diver-to-diver procedure and data resulting from the evaluation of seven diver communication systems, vis., a) Hard-line: Aquaphone; b) Acoustic: Bendix and Yack-Yack, and c) Amplitude Modulated: PQC-1a , PQC-2, Aquasonics 811 and Aquasonics 42; all systems were used with a Nautilus muzzle and a double-hose regulator.

articleTitle: Design considerations for a pulse position modulation underwater acoustic communications system
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper develops and discusses engineering design criteria for the realization of a PPM/AM underwater communications system. A number of previously unresolved questions concerning PPM/AM performance in the underwater acoustic channel are answered.

articleTitle: Ocean instrumentation: The better use of materials technology
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Manufacturers of oceanographic instrumentation seldom use current well-developed techniques for overcoming the effects of corrosion and marine fouling. The wider use of low-corrosion materials and highly effective antifoulant paint systems must await a market that is willing to underwrite the higher initial costs, but the technology is now ready for the demand.

articleTitle: Solar power on the NOMAD buoy
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: In summarizing this report it can be stated that solar energy has been effectively applied to recharge nickel cadmium and lead acid storage batteries for periods of 6 months under natural environmental conditions in tropical ocean areas. The ultimate length of time over which this energy conversion can be accomplished will be answered in continued testing. Field testing over the six month period indicates no measurable deterioration of the energy conversion system. Effectiveness of a trickle charging technique is measurable by specific gravity measurements on a large ampere-hour capacity lead-acid battery. It was not found necessary to orient the solar panels to follow the sun position and that diffused sky brightness conditions over the ocean provide many more hours of effective high level sky brightness conditions than had been anticipated. Two panels were operating during the passage of hurricanes Camille and Laurie in the storm area in the Gulf of Mexico and no deterioration in performance has been detected. Results to date indicate a possible successful correlation of solar energy panels to the measurement of fog and visibility at sea.

articleTitle: Failure mode effects and criticality analysis for system/Safety assessment
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper describes the concept and methods developed for performing a safety analysis from the viewpoint of hardware generated hazards. The FME and CA technique, originally developed for reliability oriented analyses, was expanded, refined and adapted to serve the need for a systematic, measureable and efficient method of determining the safety profile of system or equipment design.

articleTitle: Bearing accuracy with linear arrays
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper discusses the factors determining accuracy in estimating the bearing of a source using a linear array. These effects include beamwidth, sidelobes and nonhorizontal arrival angles. Both rms error and bias are considered.

articleTitle: Underwater acoustic interferometer
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Measurements have been made showing the limitations a seawater medium imposes on the resolving power of underwater acoustic equipment. An interferometer was designed that is capable of measuring the "visibility"' of the interference fringes in the far field of an acoustic radiator. Phase and amplitude fluctuations of the divided acoustic wavefront are analyzed utilizing correlation techniques.

articleTitle: High-speed automated identification and design of physical systems using hybrid computer optimization techniques
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A method has been developed for high-speed automated identification and design of linear dynamic physical systems and circuits using hybrid computer optimization techniques. The method has been extended to a specified class of nonlinear problems. Cost and speed advantages for hybrid computation over all-digital computation have been found for this class of problems. A technique of model structure optimization, believed to be original, eliminates the usual assumption of model form with the result that the optimum model form as well as the optimum parameter set is found by "growing" models. Specialized hardware developments are required for structure optimization. Results obtained by the use of these techniques and devices are presented.

articleTitle: A low light level underwater TV camera design
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Design considerations peculiar to underwater television cameras are discussed in this paper. A sensitive TV camera design is described that is suitable for diver held use and for unattended applications on manned or unmanned underseas vehicles.

articleTitle: On the application of pattern recognition techniques to oceanographic signal processing
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Pattern recognition techniques can be used in the design of computer programs for interpretation of the oceanographic seismic data. A typical pattern recognition problem is defined by feature measurements, pattern classes, and the decision rule. The physical parameters which describe the structure of the deep sea floors correspond to feature sets in pattern recognition. Examples of pattern classes are various rocks, sediments, mantles, and oceanic layers of low, medium and high porosity. The decision criterion is the minimum number of misclassifications. Specifically, the pattern recognition techniques are applied to processing of a digital seismic data tape supplied by the Woods Hole Oceanograpic Institution. A temporal array data processor combine the time-delayed data by using the stochastic approximation algorithm. Classification is then made between the recent sediments and the older eroded sediments.

articleTitle: The accuracy of multiple sensor time and bearing localization
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The performance of various transmitter configurations which are used to localize the position of a ship will be analyzed. The methods described in this paper can be applied to existing systems such as the Loran-C or OMEGA networks. They can also be used to predict the performance of a configuration prior to deployment and thus provide a means for comparing various proposed configurations.

articleTitle: Electrical insulation and breakdown characteristics of water
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A review of the insulation and breakdown characteristics of water and the factors which affect them will be presented.

articleTitle: A narrow-band multi-channel sampled data acquisition and processing system for underwater acoustic measurements
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A commercially available digital recorder, an active filter bank, and flexible programs for a general purpose digital computer have been combined, using a systems engineering approach, to realize an advance in the art of underwater acoustic experimentation. The filter bank and recorder are used as a portable narrow-band acquisition system which produces tapes for processing with a library of compatible programs.The low sampling rates required for narrow-band signals permit economical recording for long periods of time. Since actual signals, rather than derived properties are recorded, comprehensive analysis can be done.

articleTitle: Superconducting magnetometers and their potential for geophysical measurements
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The superconductive state exhibits many useful properties. Several of these, including zero electrical resistance, magnetic flux flow and Josephson tunneling are being used in the construction of very sensitive instruments for measuring magnetic fields and field derivatives. All superconducting magnetometers are vector instruments, i.e., they are sensitive to fields directed along the magnetometer axis. The superconductive element itself can be very small, on the order of 1 mm OD by 5 mm long, and straightforward dc, audio or RF electronic circuits can be used to drive the element and sense magnetic field changes.

articleTitle: General requirements for material certification of hyperbaric faults
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Certification for material adequacy of Shore Simulation Pressure Chambers is one factor to insure safety of divers and operators. Material Certification requires an independent review of design and completed hardware against a set of requirements. Material Certification Requirements discussed in this paper are applicable to both man-rated and unmanned Hyperbaric Facilities - (see definition). This discussion deals primarily with certification of a man-rated Hyperbaric Facility. An example of a non-man-rated facility is shown on Fig. 1. An example of a man-rated facility is shown on Fig. 2.

articleTitle: An unattended missile scoring system for deep and remote ocean sites
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Analog and digital data collection, processing, storage and retrieval, and acoustic telemetry techniques have been combined with undersea sonar transponder technology to produce a system for scoring missile impacts in unattended, remote, broad ocean areas. Adaptation of the system to the problem of collecting and retrieving other types of oceanographic data in similar locations is quite feasible.

articleTitle: Reliability and safety aspects of glass as a deep ocean structure
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Glass for deep ocean structres can experience local tensile stresses on the surfaces of internal bubbles even though the applied loads are compressive. To insure the safety and reliability of these structures accurate predictions of the probability of a failure originating at an internal flaw are made based on an assumed Weibull distribution of strengths. This analysis includes the effects of size and dissimilarities between the strength distributions of test specimens and the actual structure.

articleTitle: Hybrid simulation of amplitude and phase response of multielement transducer arrays
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Hybrid computational techniques, used in the simulation of realtime response of multi-element transducer arrays, are described, Computed data provide the control stimulus for amplitude and phase modulators used in the synthesis of resultant signals.

articleTitle: Instrumentation for measuring the small-scale irregularities of the sea surface and the sea bed
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A recent programme of research has been, concerned with underwater acoustic reverberation originating at the sea surface and sea bed. As part of the work involved finding a relationship between the level of the reverberation and the profile of the insonified boundary it was essential to measure the variations in height of the particular surface to a high degree of accuracy.

articleTitle: Monitoring concepts and requirements in coastal wastes management
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Those responsible and active in wastes management research, design, and operation are encouraged by the increasing public concern for the quality of the environment, particularly marine waters. The National Academy of Engineering, jointly with the National Academy of Sciences, recently completed an evaluation of the scientific and engineering requirements for research and investigation to enable further development of our ability to protect and enhance the quality of the marine environment.

articleTitle: APRES: A very low-frequency acoustic generation air compliance and pressure balancing system
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: APPRES is a novel approach to air-backed compliance for low-frequency underwater acoustic generators that provides low-impedance pressure relief at virtually any depth by means of pressure equalization with self-contained air system.

articleTitle: Marine fouling of bottom-mounted hydrophone arrays
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A facility of the Atlantic Undersea Test and Evaluation Center (AUTEC) is the weapons range which is installed on the bottom of the Tongue of the Ocean (TOTO) just east of Andros Island. The weapons range consists, in part, of bottom mounted hydrophones each individually cabled back to electronics equipment ashore. Figure 1 is a photograph of the hydrophone and its support structure just prior to be in glowered to the ocean floor on its signal cable. The hydrophone structures are implanted in water depths averaging 5000 feet, and were installed between January and July of 1966.

articleTitle: Undersea corrosion protection for aluminum structures
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper discusses a method of protecting aluminum alloy structure and instrument housings against corrosion. The abrasion-resisting qualities of hardcoat anodize are considered and the advantages of sealing the hardcoat with paint are stated. It is concluded that a hardcoat/paint combination offers a good temporary protection.

articleTitle: Correction of helium speech distortions by realtime electronic processing
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: It is well known that the use of helium in breathing gas mixtures for deep diving operations causes marked changes in speech sounds of the divers. The most prominent effect is an elevation of the formant frequencies which, in conjunction with other phenomena, progressively reduces speech intelligibility CIS depth increases.

articleTitle: A high sensitivity underwater sound velocity meter
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: An underwater sound velocity meter employing a continuous wave resonance technique is described. The device operates at a frequency of the order of 500 kHz, has a high resolution and sensitivity and is relatively immune to turbulence.

articleTitle: Considerations in the design of detectors for underwater acoustic signals
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Complicated propagation phenomena and high ambient noise in the ocean combine to make the detection of acoustic signals a difficult problem. Detection of narrowband signals, with limited duration, is of considerable importance since most uncontrolled sources emit signals of this type, and since propagation phenomena frequently preclude the use of more complex signals when controlled sources are used.

articleTitle: Management information technology for waste management and multimission oriented research
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The collection of information to manage the diverse efforts of wastes management requires special technology if management's goals are to be met. This presentation examines management information system technology used to perceive, collect, and present information for managing a research effort in pollution control or wastes management. It is demonstrated that decisionmaking structures, not computers, are the basis for management information systems.

articleTitle: Core memory digital signal processing applied to improved sonar displays
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A new sonar display uses a short-persistence phosphor CRT, driven by a digital core memory, to obviate flicker and signal compression and distortion which are characteristic of conventional, long-persistence phosphor CRTs.

articleTitle: An ocean environment simulator for studying man/Machine interactions
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The simulator will support four men and equipment, including a small submersible, in realistic ocean and habitat environments to depths of 2250 feet. Variable parameters include pressure, temperature, humidity, salinity, turbidity, and illumination.

articleTitle: A new form of gas-generating buoyancy device
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A description of compact, neutrally buoyant gas generating devices providing fail-safe recovery on command of submerged objects will be discussed in detail. A performance evaluation of an off-the-shelf gas generator providing 1000 lbs. lift at 1000 feet depth will also be discussed.

articleTitle: Plastisol coating armour wire for submarine cable
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: It is concluded that plastisol coating armouring improves elongation and revolution performances because of their large size of steel wire. In addition as the specific gravity of the cable is increased, removability of the cable on the sea bottom will be improved. The possibilities of "spew" and "kink" of the cable under practical operations will also be improved.

articleTitle: Experiences of data gathering and processing at sea
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Last year the authors were concerned with an extensive series of sea trials which had been planned to extend the knowledge of the effects of the ocean medium on propagation of acoustic pulses of varying time-bandwidth products. Propagation is used here in its widest sense referring not only to the usually measured energy loss but also to the loss of coherence in this tYPe of pulse due to the temporal and spectral spreading effects of the medium and its boundaries.

articleTitle: Electrical integrity on DEEPSTAR 20,000
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: DEEPSTAR 20,000 is a battery powered submersible vehicle with 20,000 foot depth and 16 hour dive endurance capability (See Figure 1). It is presently under construction at the Westinghouse Ocean Research and Engineering Center, located at Annapolis, Maryland.

articleTitle: Direct digital control of a high pressure life research laboratory
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This report describes planning, selection, and incorporation of a digital computer operating in the direct digital mode (DDC) for complete computer management of a large High Pressure Life Laboratory (HPLL) for deep submergence simulation to 40 atmospheres.

articleTitle: The measurement of sea surface temperature with an infrared radiometer
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The purpose of this experiment was to make simultaneous measurements of sea surface temperature with infrared and microwave radiometers. Such measurements should be useful for determining the accuracy of satellite radiometer measurements of sea surface temperatures. Measurements were made with RCA personnel as part of PROJECT ROCKFISH, at a test site on the Chesapeake Bay Bridge Tunnel near Norfolk, Virginia. Microwave and infrared radiometer measurements of the sky and water temperatures were made at various angles from the zenith down to the shoreline, at a nadir angle of<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">55\deg</tex>. A mercury thermometer and a network of floating thermistor beads were used to make simultaneous independent measurements of the water temperature. Analysis of the infrared radiometric data from Chesapeake Bay showed that for incidence or viewing angles of<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60\deg</tex>or less, the data could be corrected to within<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">\pm 1\deg</tex>C of the thermometer and thermistor data, by assuming specular reflectance at the sea surface for sky background radiation.

articleTitle: Passive microwave radiometric measurements of sea surface temperature
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Remote sensing of ocean surface and sub-surface features is of interest to a large number of ocean and marine users. Scientists, meteorologists, engineers fishermen and commercial shippers all have requirements which make remote sensing by aircraft or satellite economically practical.

articleTitle: Deep submergence photographic port
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: As undersea exploration probes greater depths, the accuracy of photographic data places more emphasis on the strength and optical quality of the pressure port through which the camera records.

articleTitle: Shallow water instrumentation: Some new concepts for expendability and economy
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Present shallow water physical and dynamic measurements are usually performed manually and are generally inefficient, costly, sparse in area coverage, and non-synoptic in observation. Some new and relatively low-cost instrumentation concepts are presented which appear to offer a practical and expedient approach to providing automatic, long-term, synoptic observations over large bay and estuary areas.

articleTitle: Underwater acoustic fixing systems
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The AC Electronics Division of General Motors Corporation has established a three-dimensional acoustic tracking range on the north edge of the Santa Cruz basin, south of the Santa Barbara Channel Islands off the California coast. The Santa Cruz Acoustic Range Facility (SCARF) contains four bottom-mounted hydrophones located in 4000 feet of water. These are cabled to an underwater termination chamber at the 6O-foot depth. Additional cables lead from the chamber to the control center located on Santa Cruz Island. The system will track a target in 3 dimensions in the spherical mode using three hydrophones within a circle 25,000 feet in diameter with an rms error of less than 10 feet. In the hyperbolic mode the system will track in three dimensions over an ellipse1 5,000 feet by 5000 feet to a rms accuracy of 10 feet and an ellipse 30,000 feet by 10,000 feet for an rms error of 30 feet.

articleTitle: A fishfinding sonar utilizing an audio information display
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A wide beam, forward looking, FM sonar using a purely audio information display, derived from twin receiving arrays, is described. The system was developed with the aim of providing an effective, but inexpensive, sonar for fishfinding. Preliminary sea trials with this system have indicated that accurate target tracking may be achieved without scanning of the transducers, and that the detection capability of the system, is considerable.

articleTitle: TRACE: A mechanism for acoustic simulation
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Several years ago Honeywell's Marine Systems Center in Seattle started work on aprogram to develop an acoustic signal processor for an underwater vehicle. We were aware that refraction and reflection of the direct signal from the surface and the bottom would yield multiple signals and that refraction, although ever-present, cannot be accurately predicted. It became apparent that on certain days processors operating in thew ater seemed to behave abnormally. Attempting to correlate this abnormal behavior with known conditions, we found indications that a combination of reflection and refraction, producing multiple signal paths, might cause the noted abnormalities. A search of existing literature shed little light upon the effects of multiple signal paths on the performance of an acoustic signal processor. As a result the authors developed TRACE, a fast and economical means for evaluating the effectiveness of underwater vehicles in a realistically simulated undersea environment. The Honeywell TRACE facility has proved its effectiveness in analyzing design parameters and verifying actual performance of sonar-guided underwater vehicles. A unique feature of the TRACE facility is that it subjects acoustic signal processors to a multiplicity of signals occurring in the acoustic environment as a result of refraction and reflection. This paper describes TRACE, including some of the models used and the hardware designed to implement those models.

articleTitle: Space sensors application to synoptic oceanography
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Traditionally, man's knowledge about his ocean environment has been acquired by point sampling, generally from surface ships. Because of the relatively few number of ships available for conducting oceanographic surveys, and the hostile nature of the ocean itself, the data acquired has been costly in terms of money and time. Further, the dynamic nature and behavior of the seas requires that observations be synoptic rather than point observations which have been separated widely in time and space.

articleTitle: Hydrodynamics of launching, suspension and retrieval of heavy loads in deep ocean through cable from floating platform in rough seas
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: One of the important tasks among various ocean engineering activities is to lower, suspend and raise a heavy equipment in the deep ocean from a ship or a moored platform through a cable or cables in rough seas. A new theory of this dynamic system is developed and a method of quantitative solution for irregular sea waves is presented.

articleTitle: Remote monitoring of critical physiological factors of the saturated diver
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Saturated divers are as completely separated from surface support personnel as an astronaut on the moon is from mission control. While determing the aquanaut's condition is at least as important, since in some respects he is operating in a more hostile environment, our present ability to remotely monitor the aquanaut's condition is more limited than that which NASA has achieved with the astronaut. For the long term, advances are required in the state - of - the - art of sensing elements and voice communications. For the immediate future application of existing technology and repackaging is required to safely exploit the demonstrated technique of saturated diving.

articleTitle: The submerged insulated traveling-wave antenna
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A linear Insulated antenna that is useful for underwater communication has been developed, analyzed, and tested experimentally. It utilizes a traveling-wave behavior to achieve useful directivity and gain.

articleTitle: Parameter considerations for magnetic sensor instrumentation
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The following presentation attempts to summarize the main interrelationships between the application and device aspects of magnetic anomaly detectors and/or locators. The discussion is founded on an eleven-year research, design and development program primarily directed toward underwater, swimmer portable, locator systems. Productive discussions of magnetic sensor techniques are frequently hindered by the lack of uniform and standard terms of reference. No reference is made in this text to system sensitivity or range because these terms are useless and misleading unless they are accompanied by numerous clarifying details. The authors are convinced that a consistent and comprehensive dialogue would greatly enhance progress in the field of magnetic anomaly detection and instrumentation. We hope that this effort encourages other investigators to seek out, publish, and use standard terms of reference.

articleTitle: An enclosure (Junction box) for passive electronics installed in near shore ocean bottom implantment
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: It is my intention to describe the action taken to provide protection for an installation which has been placed in a rigorous ocean environment. The equipment to be described is a junction box for submarine communications cables. The box is secured to the ocean bottom at 60 foot depth off a tropical beach. Figure 1

articleTitle: The beamformer as a log-likelihood ratio detector
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Some basic relationships are presented among the likelihood ratio, the Bryn statistic and the beamformer output when detecting plane waves using an array. Particular attention is paid to output shape versus steering in each case.

articleTitle: Modeling of the surface scattering channel as a time-varying stochastic filter
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: In this paper an attempt is made to relate the so called "microscopic" and "macroscopic" approaches used to analyze an undersea acoustic channel, consisting of a set of correlated scatterers, distributed over a slowly time-varying random surface.

articleTitle: An approach to acquisition and handling of serial environmental data
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Attention has recently been focused on management programs for coastal waste control. A requirement in developing such programs is a thorough understanding of the environmental parameters operating in the coastal zone. Specification of the parameters of interest is not sufficient. Their spatial and temporal variations and their interrelationships must be measured.

articleTitle: Optical (infrared and ultraviolet-visual) remote sensing of pollution of water bodies
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: This paper presents some recent results from experimentation to develop means of remoteq lensing material and the:nnal pollution of water bodies and concludes with some general remarks regarding the likely future course of such developments.

articleTitle: Achievable performance of acoustic imaging systems
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Image information content, sonar equations for different target types, and achievable range-resolution performance envelopes are presented. Potential for improved performance and versatility through non linear techniques is explored. Illustrations from experiments are provided.

articleTitle: A two-compartment chamber for long-term animal studies at gaseous pressures up to forty atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A high pressure chamber for long-term animal experimentation is described. A gate valve separates two compartments, each can be held at pressures up to forty atmospheres. Controlled parameters are: temperature, humidity, and gaseous composition.

articleTitle: Nuclear power sources for underwater application
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Past, present, and future nuclear power sources for Navy underwater applications are discussed. Actual undersea nuclear power installations are illustrated. Data describing the availability, power characteristics, and cost effectiveness of underwater power sources are presented.

articleTitle: Design and performance of undersea electroacoustic hardware for corrosion and biofouling protection
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Subject report deals with the job of designing electroacoustic hardware to function according to plan in the undersea environment. Design techniques and rationale are described, and limited performance records are given. The designs and techniques discussed were developed over a span of several years and were influenced by basic corrosion and biofouling studies conducted in Governmnent laboratories; these techniques have been made available to the industry and have been incorporated in hardware with reasonable success.

articleTitle: Some approaches to the problem of current interruption in deep-submergence applications
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A problem in the development of deep-diving vehicles under the Navy's Deep Ocean Technology (DOT) program is that of circuit interruption. Devices used for on-off switching and for circuit protection are, when possible, mounted outside the pressure hull of a vessel for optimum weight and space saving. Protection from the surrounding sea environment is readily obtained by immersion in a dielectric fluid inside a thinwalled enclosure called a pressure compensating chamber, which is flexible to allow for fluid compression at great depths. The initial use of switches in pressure-compensating chambers showed frequent failure by the build-up of solid material, referred to as "clinkers", on switch contacts. At the Naval Ship Research and Development Laboratory in Annapolis, it was decided to take a closer look at the contact failure problem and attempt to provide technology for the design of circuit-interrupting devices applicable to future deep-ocean vehicle systems.

articleTitle: Engineering responsibilities in protecting the environment while developing ocean resources
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: It took the experiences of Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl t o make the world sit up and take notice of just how polluted our waters are. No longer is it necessary to visit an industrialized city or sail down a commercial artery to see the effects our technologically advanced, no deposit-no return society is having on the environment. The evidence has drifted right out into the middle of our oceans. The disastrous consequences are there for all to see.

articleTitle: Electrical insulating materials for deep submergence applications
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Investigations of electrical insulating materials immersed in dielectric fluids when subjected to environmental conditions to simulate deep submergence applications are discussed.

articleTitle: Holographic acoustic imaging for underwater viewing
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Ultrasonic holograms of objects as small as 0.25" in diameter have been made in water at 5 feet using 5 MHz. High-resolution images have been constructed from such holograms using optical and computer techniques.

articleTitle: Electrical insulation of an AC propulsion motor for the DEEPSTAR 20,000
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The DEEPSTAR 20,000 vehicle will be propelled by an a-c induction motor designed for light weight, reliable operation at depths to 20,000 feet. It is a 2-pole a-c squirrel-cage induction motor which operates at a speed of 3450 rpm at full load, developing 10 horsepower at 60 hertz at 20,000 feet. The voltage established for 60 Hz operation is 82 V ac line-to-line. It is delta connected internally for a high order of system efficiency and compatibility with the controller. The motor operates in a petroleum based fluid maintained at a slight positive internal pressure relative to ambient. The motor windings are polyimide-enameled copper wire impregnated with diphenyl oxide resin varnish. Slot and ground insulation is polyimide film bonded on both sides of polyamide fiber paper, totaling about 10 mils in thickness. The insulation system offers reliable electrical operation with effective cooling characteristics when operated under load. Testing has been performed on this design in air, oil, and seawater-contaminated oil. The conditions of the peformance tests included sea level, hydraulic pressures up to 13,500 psi, and repeated cycling between the extremes.

articleTitle: Estuary parameter measurements and data handling - A new approach using underwater sound telemetry
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: A multiple-parameter measurement and data acquisition system for synoptic data collection over shallow water areas is described. This system will make use of low-cost remote sensor/telemetry modules which relay data to intermediate shore-based stations by underwater sound telemetry. The remote modules will initiate multiple-parameter measurements on command from the shore stations. After reception of the telemetered acoustic signals at each shore station, the data from the shore stations are relayed to a central collection point. The implementation of this design concept will provide synoptic measurements over sectors of 1 to 2 miles in radius around each shore station for a period from 6 to 12 months, thus providing information at a very low cost per data point.

articleTitle: Underwater lighting
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Increased interest in working on the ocean floor has been accompanied by the need for better underwater illumination. Artificial illumination is required in deep water where ambient light is limited and in shallow water where work must be done at night. In the past, where decreased mobility and small area illumination were acceptable, the hand-held, or swimmer-mounted, lights were adequate. These older methods of illumination are obsolescent with the requirements for increased swimmer mobility and larger areas of illumination. Most commercially available underwater lights do not lend themselves well to large area illumination due to high cost and small angular beam spread.

articleTitle: Reliability and safety aspects of delivering and detonating large explosive charges undersea
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The IIT Research Institute recently completed the undersea detonation of a 250-ton explosive charge in the North Pacific for the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA). The cylindrical steel container constructed for the program was loaded with 243 tons of slurry explosive at Port Madison, near Seattle. The container was towed 2600 nm to its test location, 26 mi from Amchitka in the Aleutian Islands. The container was boarded, armed and scuttled at the test site. Data reduction indicated full explosive yield was achieved at the planned depth. Failure of some key contingency equipment (remote scuttle capability and secondary detonators) during the tow to the Aleutians led to a thorough review and reevaluation of the reliability and safety to the system. New techniques were sought to deal with the problem of safety and reliability. The purpose of the analysis was to determine those areas where additional or special effort may be required to insure a safe and successful completion of the mission.

articleTitle: Calculations of the signal/Noise ratio in underwater optical heterodyne detection systems
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: The development of high intensity lasers operating in the blue - green portion of the spectrum has given new impetus to the application of these lasers to problems of underwater detection and communication. One of the advantages of a laser source over an incandescent source is the spatial coherence property of the laser. Previous work1 has shown that the spatial coherence properties of the laser radiation are not adversely affected upon propagation through water. Therefore, it is of interest to compare the performance of an optical heterodyne detection system, which utilizes the spatial coherence properties of the radiation to be detected, with that of a direct detection system. A comparative analysis of direct detection systems and heterodyne detection systems is presented for operation in typical lake water as characterized by Duntley.2 For both systems, the maximum detection range, defined as the range at which it can be determined whether an infinite extent white target is present, is calculated for both diffusely reflecting and specularly reflecting targets. The criterion for comparing the two systems is the signal-to-noise ratio, and while the maximum range estimates for the two systems should be fairly accurate, it must be pointed out that for an operating system the maximum detection range may vary by several orders of magnitude depending on the water and target parameters.

articleTitle: Underwater acoustic imaging: An assessment of feasibility
publicationTitle: 1970 IEEE International Conference on Engineering in the Ocean Environment - Digest of Technical Papers
abstract: Ideally, an ultrasonic imaging system operating in the reflective mode would construct a recognizable two-dimensional image of an object in the presence of various disturbances any of which, in the absence of adequate detail, could be erroneously identified as the object itself. The final output of any such imaging system may be considered as a two-dimensional array of independent information elements; the number of image elements, in general, equaling the total number of information channels. The elements may use a common carrier either in part or in the entirety on their respective transmission channels. In all cases there is a transmitter, an object to be visualized, an electro-acoustic receiving device, an amplifier system, and an electro-optical display. It is concluded that it does appear possible to design an imaging system which uses both the diffuse and specular components of the backscattered ultrasonic energy from a submerged object that will yield detail and shape information superior to that obtained by specular return alone. A reasonable range for a compact system appears to be about 30 meters. Two major physical limitations are: 1. The extremely low diffuse power reflected from the relatively smooth targets which are anticipated, and 2. The large specular-to-diffuse reflected power ratio which can result in 11blooming11 due to the finite aperture of the imaging system.
